Take a photograph and make a photocopy. Then a photocopy of the
photocopy. Do it again. And again.

If you keep going long enough, the picture is gone. What's on the page
is grey noise that could plausibly have started as almost anything. The
information about the original has been erased.

This is a familiar form of loss. Each pass through the copier loses a
little, the losses pile up, and eventually nothing remains. Heat works
this way too. So does mixing dye into water, or scrambling a Rubik's
cube, or letting milk cool in a glass. Everywhere you look, processes
that destroy information are processes that destroy it in *steps*:
many small irreversible nudges that add up.

Now think about how you'd design such a process. You have full control
of the photocopier. The cheap thing you can do is make it violently
destructive: a single pass turns any input into grey noise. Erasure in
one step. Done.

You can also build copiers that never quite finish in any finite number
of passes, and only erase everything in the infinite limit of repeated
copying. This is a genuinely interesting region of design space.
Characterising which copiers really do erase everything in the limit
(as opposed to settling onto some non-trivial steady image, or
oscillating, or simply slowing to a crawl) is the subject of a
substantial literature on ergodic and mixing channels.[^mixing-ref] It
is not, however, the question of this post.

This post's question sits between those two. How *slowly* can you
erase, while still finishing in finitely many steps?

Concretely: among all copy-of-a-copy operations that erase the
original after some exact number $k$ of identical applications, how
large can $k$ be?

[^mixing-ref]: TODO: pick one of the candidate references suggested in
chat (e.g. Burgarth et al. 2013 on ergodic/mixing channels, or Sanz et
al. 2010 on the quantum Wielandt inequality), or Michael Wolf's
*Quantum Channels & Operations: Guided Tour* lecture notes for a more
pedagogical entry point.

That largest $k$ is where this post lives, and it has different answers
in different settings. If the copier has to behave like a classical
probabilistic process, you get one bound. Upgrade to quantum mechanics,
and the bound becomes *quadratically* larger. Then restrict the quantum
copier to a tightly constrained, low-parameter family of operations, a
family with vastly less freedom than the general quantum case, and you
might expect the bound to drop most of the way back down.

It almost doesn't. The factor-of-2 gap that remains is the punchline.
The reason it remains is a piece of finite-field bookkeeping that
turns out, if you sit with it, to be unreasonably beautiful.

<!-- =================================================================== -->
## The classical setup {#sec-classical}

Let's make the photocopier mathematically precise. We start with the
classical case, where everything is ordinary probability theory.

Pick a small number of distinct states that your image can be in. Say
there are three: black, grey, and white. Then "the image" at any
moment is described by a probability distribution over these three
states. Maybe right now the image is definitely white,
$p = (0, 0, 1)$. Maybe after some processing it has drifted to
$p = (0.4, 0.5, 0.1)$, meaning the image is 40% likely black, 50%
grey, 10% white, with the uncertainty representing whatever noise has
crept in.

The set of all such probability distributions over $d$ states is a
familiar geometric object: a $(d - 1)$-dimensional simplex. For
$d = 3$ it is a triangle. The corners are the pure states (definitely
this colour, no uncertainty), and the centre is the uniform
distribution (totally unsure, every colour equally likely).

![**Figure 1.** The $d = 3$ probability simplex, drawn as a triangle.
Vertices are the pure states; the centre is the uniform
distribution.](figures/simplex-d3.svg){#fig-simplex-d3}

A copy operation takes one probability distribution and returns
another. The mathematical object that does this is a *stochastic
matrix*: a $d \times d$ matrix $S$ whose columns are themselves
probability distributions. Column $j$ tells you "if the input is
definitely state $j$, here is the probability distribution of the
output." And $S$ acts on a general distribution $p$ by matrix
multiplication: $Sp$ is the output distribution.

Two facts about stochastic matrices are worth pinning down before we
keep going. First, $S^k$ describes what happens if you apply $S$ to
its own output $k$ times in a row, so the question of finite roots is
going to be a question about powers of matrices. Second, the entries
of $S^k$ stay non-negative and the columns still sum to one, so no
matter how many times you copy, the result is still a stochastic
matrix and still maps the simplex to the simplex. Nothing escapes.

Now we can say precisely what "total erasure" means. The most
depolarising copier you can write down is the one whose every column
is the uniform distribution. Every input state, no matter which one,
produces the same uniform output:
$$
P = \frac{1}{d}\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1 \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
1 & 1 & \cdots & 1
\end{pmatrix}.
$$

Apply $P$ to anything and you get the uniform distribution back. All
information about the input has been thrown away in a single step.
Apply $P$ again and nothing changes; the simplex has been crushed to a
single point, the centre, and $P$ just keeps mapping it there.

This $P$ is the *completely depolarising channel*, or CDC. (More
precisely it is the *bistochastic* CDC, the one that preserves the
uniform distribution. There are other CDCs that crush the simplex to
some other fixed point. For the rest of this post, "CDC" will always
mean the bistochastic one.)

With $P$ pinned down we can ask the post's question, precisely. A
*$k$-th root* of $P$ is a stochastic matrix $S$ such that
$$
S^k = P \quad \text{and} \quad S^r \ne P \text{ for any } r < k.
$$
The second condition is just "the erasure really happens at step $k$,
not earlier." How large can $k$ be?

The answer is sharp: $k \leq d - 1$.

The proof is a piece of standard linear algebra. The Jordan
decomposition of $S$ pins down what its $k$-th power can look like,
and the constraint that $S^k$ equals the rank-one matrix $P$ leaves
exactly the room you'd expect. The geometric picture is simpler. The
simplex is $(d - 1)$-dimensional. Each application of $S$ can collapse
at most one of those independent dimensions of variance without
overshooting and erasing the whole thing prematurely. After $d - 1$
collapses there is nothing left for the next step to do, and you have
arrived at $P$.[^classical-bound-proof]

[^classical-bound-proof]: TODO: cite the Jordan-block argument for
the classical case (Section 2.5 / 3.1.3 of the thesis, or a standard
reference on roots of stochastic matrices).

For $d = 2$ the bound says $k = 1$, which is to say there are no
non-trivial roots. The two-state CDC can only be split into one step,
itself. Total erasure of one classical bit is a one-shot affair.

For $d = 3$ the bound is $k = 2$. A square root of the bistochastic
$3 \times 3$ CDC exists, and it acts on the simplex by funnelling
every point along a two-step trajectory to the centre.

![**Figure 2.** A square root $S$ of the $d = 3$ bistochastic CDC,
visualised on the simplex. A starting distribution is mapped to an
intermediate point by $S$, and then to the centre by a second
application of $S$. The map $S^2 = P$ collapses every starting point
to the centre in exactly two steps.](figures/simplex-root-d3.svg){#fig-root-d3}

And that is the classical story. A clean bound, a clean construction,
and not much more to say about it.

The interesting thing is what happens to that bound when we let
ourselves leave classical probability behind.

## The quantum upgrade {#sec-quantum}

If qubits, gates, and the $|0\rangle, |1\rangle$ notation aren't
already part of your mental furniture, the gentlest on-ramp I know of
is Matuschak and Nielsen's
[Quantum Computing for the Very Curious](https://quantum.country/qcvc).
Read it first, or just keep going and chase the link when something
looks unfamiliar.

## Clifford channels as the playground {#sec-clifford}

## The reduction (the pivot) {#sec-reduction}

<!-- TODO: This is the "wait, what just happened?" moment — give it air.
  - Compute $T^n[\mathbf{w}(\eta)]$:
    $\prod_{k=0}^{n-1} \lambda(h^k(\eta)) \, \mathbf{w}(h^n(\eta))$.
  - The action on Weyl labels is just $h^n$ — a linear map on
    $\mathbb{F}_d^2$ — and the accumulated phase is a product of $\lambda$
    values along the orbit.
  - Conclusion: the question "is $T$ a $k$-th root of the CDC?" reduces to
    a question about (a) the order of $h$ and (b) where $\lambda$
    vanishes along orbits.
  - The channel question has become a question about finite-dimensional
    linear algebra over $\mathbb{F}_d$.
-->
